1141.event_title: The 'Mitchy boom' greets Crown Prince Akihito's engagement to Michiko Shoda
1141.event: Crown Prince Akihito met Michiko Shoda, the daughter of a flour-milling businessman, at a tennis match in Karuizawa in the summer of 1957, and the Imperial Household Agency announced their engagement in November 1958. Some conservatives objected to a commoner becoming crown princess, but the public took her to heart: a 'Mitchy boom' swept the country, women's magazines covered her closely, and television sales doubled as people prepared to watch the wedding. They married on 10 April 1959 before crowds of more than half a million along the parade route.
1141.explanation: The public's warm talk and enthusiasm surrounded a match that broke with tradition and gave it strong popular support.
1141.tie_back: In the kural the lover says that the town's gossip about the romance is what keeps him alive; for Akihito and Michiko, the nation's eager talk was a source of strength rather than shame.
1141._accuracy_note: Public talk clearly favoured the couple, but the kural's alar is village gossip about a secret courtship, whereas this was open national celebration of an announced engagement.

1142.event_title: Tennyson and Emily Sellwood part, and a story spreads to explain it
1142.event: Alfred Tennyson became engaged to Emily Sellwood in the late 1830s, but in 1840 the engagement was broken off. Accounts differ on why: one says her family ended it after he lost money in a bad investment, while another says Tennyson himself broke it off over money and fears about his family's health, and that a story was put about that her father had forbidden the match in order to spare Emily embarrassment. They were reunited and married quietly in 1850, shortly after In Memoriam was published.
1142.explanation: Talk about a broken engagement could shape how a couple was seen, yet their bond survived ten years apart.
1142.tie_back: The kural's lover is grateful that the town's rumour has linked him with the girl it does not know is so hard to win; Tennyson and Emily's story shows how what people said about a courtship could serve a purpose of its own.
1142._accuracy_note: Next-best only: a rumour did surround the broken engagement, but it protected the woman's reputation rather than helping the lover as in the kural, and the two sources disagree on who ended the engagement.

1143.event_title: Longfellow keeps hoping for six years after Fanny Appleton's refusal
1143.place: Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
1143.event: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow fell in love with Frances (Fanny) Appleton after travelling with her family in Switzerland, and was crushed when she rejected his marriage proposal in 1837. He resumed his friendship with her in Cambridge and Boston, and she finally accepted him in the spring of 1843. They married in July 1843, and her father gave them Craigie House as a wedding present.
1143.explanation: For years Longfellow lived on the hope of a union he had not yet won, before it finally came true.
1143.tie_back: The kural's lover says that hearing the town's talk makes his heart feel as though it already has the union it has not yet gained; Longfellow's long hope shows a heart living on a union still to come.
1143._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the waiting heart fits, but no public rumour is documented in Longfellow's courtship; this event is also used for kural 1132.

1144.event_title: Rumours of Crown Prince Harald's chosen bride spark a national debate
1144.event: Crown Prince Harald and Sonja Haraldsen, a commoner, had been a couple for many years before rumours spread in 1967 and 1968 of a girlfriend he wished to marry. Newspapers and the public debated whether a commoner could become queen, while Harald made clear that if he could not marry Sonja he would consider staying single for life. King Olav V sought political advice and finally consented, and the couple married on 29 August 1968.
1144.explanation: Once the romance became the subject of public talk, it moved from a private hope toward an open, accepted marriage.
1144.tie_back: The kural says love blossoms on the town's gossip and would wither without it; Harald and Sonja's love, once talked about by the whole country, grew into a public marriage rather than fading.
1144._accuracy_note: The couple's love was strong before the rumours, so the talk did not make it grow; this event is also used for kural 1138.

1145.event_title: John Lennon and Yoko Ono turn their honeymoon into a Bed-In
1145.event: John Lennon and Yoko Ono married in Gibraltar on 20 March 1969 and, knowing the wedding would draw press attention, spent their honeymoon in bed at the Amsterdam Hilton from 25 to 31 March. Every day from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. they invited reporters into the room, where they sat in pyjamas talking about peace. A second week-long Bed-In followed in Montreal, where the song Give Peace a Chance was recorded.
1145.explanation: Rather than hide their new marriage from the press, the couple invited the world in, again and again.
1145.tie_back: The kural compares love made public to drink that grows sweeter each time; Lennon and Ono made their love public twice over and welcomed the attention rather than shrinking from it.
1145._accuracy_note: The couple embraced publicity around their marriage, but they used it mainly to promote peace, not to deepen their love.

1146.event_title: Princess Margaret's romance with Peter Townsend becomes known to all
1146.place: London, United Kingdom, and Brussels, Belgium
1146.event: Princess Margaret wished to marry Group Captain Peter Townsend, a divorced royal equerry, but under the Royal Marriages Act she needed the queen's permission, and the Church of England did not accept remarriage after divorce. Townsend was posted overseas as an air attaché, and after the two met again in October 1955 she publicly announced that she would not marry him. Her decision was made known in a public statement setting out her reasons.
1146.explanation: A private love quickly became a matter that everyone discussed and that touched Church and state.
1146.tie_back: In the kural the heroine says she saw her lover only once, yet the rumour has spread like news of an eclipse; Margaret's romance likewise became known far beyond the people involved.
1146._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the wide public knowledge fits, but the relationship lasted years rather than one meeting, and the sources checked do not describe the press coverage in detail; this event is also used for kural 1137.

1147.event_title: Sir George More's fury fails to undo John Donne's marriage
1147.event: In December 1601 John Donne secretly married Ann More, the young niece of Lady Egerton. When Donne told her father, Sir George More, some months later, he reacted with fury, sought an annulment, refused a dowry and had Donne dismissed from his post as Sir Thomas Egerton's secretary and briefly imprisoned. The marriage was nevertheless upheld, More was eventually reconciled to his son-in-law, and the couple stayed together, raising a large family.
1147.explanation: A parent's anger and the scandal around a secret match did not break the marriage; the couple held together through years of hardship.
1147.tie_back: The kural says the town's gossip is the manure and the mother's harsh words the water that make love-sickness grow; for Donne and Ann, a parent's fury and the scandal only bound them more firmly to the life they had chosen.
1147._accuracy_note: A parent's angry opposition fits well, but it was the bride's father rather than her mother, and the sources do not say that the opposition increased their love; this event is also used for kural 1133.

1148.event_title: The Lovings' marriage outlasts banishment and reaches the Supreme Court
1148.place: Caroline County, Virginia, and Washington, D.C., United States
1148.event: Richard and Mildred Loving married in Washington, D.C., on 2 June 1958, were arrested at home in Virginia under its ban on interracial marriage, and in January 1959 were sentenced to a year in prison, suspended on condition that they leave the state. They moved to Washington but kept fighting, and the American Civil Liberties Union took up their case. On 12 June 1967 the United States Supreme Court unanimously struck down Virginia's law.
1148.explanation: Punishment and public condemnation did not end the marriage; instead the couple's struggle changed the law of the whole country.
1148.tie_back: The kural says that trying to put out love with gossip is like pouring ghee on a fire; every attempt to break the Lovings apart only made their marriage a larger cause.
1148._accuracy_note: Opposition clearly failed to extinguish the couple's love, though they faced law and courts rather than village gossip; this event is also used for kural 1140.

1149.event_title: Kierkegaard breaks his engagement to Regine Olsen
1149.event: Søren Kierkegaard became engaged to Regine Olsen on 10 September 1840, but soon decided that he could not marry her. Despite her strong opposition, he broke the engagement for good on 12 October 1841, causing her great despair and provoking widespread indignation in Copenhagen, and he left for Berlin for a time. Regine married Johan Frederik Schlegel in 1847, and Kierkegaard, who never married, left her his remaining possessions in his will.
1149.explanation: A promise of marriage was withdrawn in a way that exposed the young woman to public talk, though she later built her own life.
1149.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that the man who once told her not to fear has left her shamed before many, so why should she still fear the town's gossip; Regine was left by her betrothed in a break that all Copenhagen discussed.
1149._accuracy_note: The abandonment before many people fits, but Regine's own words about the gossip are not recorded in the sources, and the kural's hero later returns while Kierkegaard did not; already used once elsewhere in the book (chapter 121).

1150.event_title: Bertha Kinsky secretly marries Arthur von Suttner and leaves with him for the Caucasus
1150.event: Bertha Kinsky became engaged to Baron Arthur von Suttner, seven years her junior, but his family strongly opposed the match, so in 1876 she took a post in Paris as secretary to Alfred Nobel. After only a week or so she returned to Vienna, secretly married Arthur, and the couple left at once for the Caucasus, where they lived for nine years by teaching and writing. In 1885 they returned to Austria, welcomed by his now relenting family; she later won the 1905 Nobel Peace Prize.
1150.explanation: Faced with family opposition, the couple chose to marry and leave together, and in time the family accepted them.
1150.tie_back: In the kural the confidante urges the couple to go away together, sure that the lover will agree; Bertha and Arthur did just that, marrying secretly and leaving together despite his family's opposition.
1150._accuracy_note: A real case of a couple marrying secretly and leaving together, but no rumour is documented as the trigger, which is central to the kural.
